caption:
The companies behind Elvis Presley's and Eminem's songs sued AI music app Suno on November 6.
They say Suno copied hundreds of their songs to train its AI and lets users make tracks that sound like the real thing.
Eminem's publisher could seek more than $40 million. Suno says it bans prompts with artists' names.

Should AI music apps pay the artists they learned from?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: CBS News, The Daily Star · Photo: The Daily Star
threads_text: The owners of Elvis Presley's and Eminem's songs just sued Suno, the AI app that writes full songs from a text prompt. One complaint says Suno spit out a track called "Lose Yourself by Eminem" with the real lyrics. Should AI music apps have to pay the artists they trained on?

site_article.headline: Elvis Presley and Eminem rights holders sue AI music company Suno
site_article.dek: Two complaints filed on the same day in California say Suno trained on hundreds of their songs and lets users make music that imitates them.
site_article.summary: Eminem's publisher Eight Mile Style and a group of Elvis Presley rights holders filed separate copyright suits against AI music generator Suno on November 6, 2026. The Eminem complaint covers 269 songs and could seek more than $40 million.
site_article.seo_title: Elvis and Eminem rights holders sue AI music app Suno
site_article.seo_description: Eight Mile Style and Elvis Presley rights holders filed suits against Suno, saying it trained on their songs and imitates Presley's voice.
site_article.answer_summary: Eminem's publisher and Elvis Presley's rights holders say Suno copied their songs to train its AI music generator without permission. Suno says it bans prompts that name artists or songs.

paragraphs.text: Two sets of music rights holders sued Suno, the company behind a popular AI song generator, on November 6, 2026. One suit was filed by Eight Mile Style, the Michigan publisher that owns or controls a large part of Eminem's catalog. The other was filed by a group of Elvis Presley rights holders that includes Authentic Brands Group and Raleigh Music Publishing. Both cases were brought in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, according to CBS News and The Daily Star.

Eight Mile Style says Suno infringed 269 musical compositions it owns or controls. The complaint lists direct copyright infringement, circumvention of protection measures, and removal or alteration of copyright management information. It says Suno made illicit copies of millions of copyrighted works and trained its model so users can create recordings from text prompts, CBS News reported.

One example in the filing describes a track that Suno generated under the title "Lose Yourself by Eminem," which the publisher says copies the lyrics of the original song verbatim. FourWeekMBA, citing the Detroit Free Press, reported that the complaint also points to lyrics from "The Real Slim Shady" and "Houdini." Eminem himself is not a plaintiff.

The suit also claims that Suno used a service to scrape songs and lyrics from YouTube Music, Deezer and Genius, a claim CBS News attributed to earlier reporting by 404 Media. The publisher asks the court to find that the infringement was willful, to order unauthorized copies impounded or destroyed, and to award damages that CBS News said could exceed $40 million. According to FourWeekMBA, the figure comes from $150,000 for each of the 269 songs, the maximum for willful infringement, plus about $672,000 tied to removed copyright information.
The Presley case and the ELVIS Act

The Presley complaint runs 51 pages and says Suno copied 859 of the singer's compositions to train its system, The Daily Star reported. It also says users can generate music that imitates Presley's voice and likeness, and it invokes Tennessee's ELVIS Act, a 2024 law that protects performers against unauthorized commercial use of their voice and image. The filing warns that "The next Elvis won't pick up a guitar."
Both cases were filed by the same legal team, which includes attorney Richard Busch, who previously represented Marvin Gaye's estate in the "Blurred Lines" case.

In a statement to CBS News, Suno said it exists to help people create new, original music and not to trade on anyone's name or likeness. The company said it prohibits unauthorized use of an artist's work, does not allow prompts for specific artists' names and songs, and works with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio and lyrics. Suno already faces claims from Universal Music Group and Sony Music Entertainment, while Warner Music Group settled its case last year.

The two suits test different ideas. The Eminem case is a classic copyright fight over training data and copied lyrics, while the Presley case leans on a newer kind of law that protects a voice itself. If a court accepts the voice claim, AI music companies could face limits on what their tools sound like, not only on what they were trained on.
The next step to watch is Suno's formal answer in the Northern District of California, and whether the court lets the ELVIS Act claim proceed alongside the copyright counts.
